abstract: Small mammals and large herbivores have co-evolved in grasslands for millions of years, yet how they interact remains unclear. Although large herbivores can significantly affect the smaller ones, the reverse effect is largely unknown. On the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, plateau pikas (Ochotona curzoniae) are often considered pests that compete with livestock at high densities. Using field experiments, we show that the presence of pikas facilitates weight gains of yaks (Bos grunniens) by improving vegetation composition at a moderate density level. Compared to the pika-present treatment, pika removal dramatically increased cover of the poisonous Stellera forbs by twofold, reducing the abundance and protein content of palatable grasses and sedges, yak foraging efficiency, and yak weight gain by up to 42%. Notably, we found a humped relationship between yak weight gains and pika burrow densities in the pika-present plots; the facilitative effect of pikas on yaks was highest at about 200 burrows/ha, but shifted to a competitive effect at pika densities exceeding 400 burrows/ha. These results provide the first empirical evidence that maintaining a moderate density of small mammalian herbivores can benefit growth performance of livestock by improving vegetation composition. Our study highlights the significance of moderate populations of ecosystem-engineering small mammals in sustaining pastoral productivity in rangelands.

EnglandElife1015796142050-084XIMdoi: 10.64898/2026.04.06.716644doi: 10.7554/eLife.111340.1doi: 10.7554/eLife.111340.2AnimalsLagomorphaphysiologyHerbivoryGrasslandCattlegrowth & developmentPopulation DensityLivestockgrowth & developmentOn the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau, yaks share alpine meadows with a small herbivore, the plateau pika. Opinions about the role of pikas are divided. Some see them as serious pests because they compete with yaks for forage and destroy pastureland, causing land degradation and damage to livestock production. Others see them as a keystone species because they play an important role in maintaining ecosystem health as ecosystem engineers and as prey for many predators. However, no one has ever tested these opposing views. Pikas frequently clip (but do not eat) the tall poisonous weed Stellera. Stellera has expanded massively under grazing pressure, outcompeting palatable grasses and sedges and thereby threatening yak health. Pikas may thus indeed benefit livestock production by removing this poisonous weed. Zhong et al. wanted to test the hypothesis that at moderate densities, pika may improve yak body growth by suppressing poisonous Stellera plants, but at high densities they may inhibit yak body growth by competing with yaks for food. Using manipulative field experiments, the researchers found that pikas cut down tall Stellera plants, reducing their cover by half. This released grasses and sedges from competition, increasing their abundance and crude protein content by 14%, and improved yak foraging efficiency by 30-40%. Consequently, yak daily weight gain increased by up to 42% in the presence of pikas. Importantly, the relationship was hump-shaped: benefits peaked at ~200 pika burrows per hectare but turned negative above ~400 burrows per hectare. The study of Zhong et al. shows that moderate pika densities can enhance livestock production by improving forage quality. Local herders and rangeland managers could benefit by moving from an indiscriminate pika eradication strategy to density-based pika management, maintaining pikas at moderate levels (below ~400 burrows/ha) to boost yak growth while preventing outbreaks. However, further research is needed to test whether similar facilitation occurs at higher elevations (>4,000 m), during winter seasons, or with other livestock (e.g., sheep).
